status: model reading, pending operator review (not a gate decision)
statement_tested: Table A1 row: Depression status is associated with MCI, but whether depression severity grades MCI neurobiology and prognosis is divided in this corpus: within the supporting studies, continuous severity scores fail to track brain measures or conversion, although in one of them major-depression groups had lower functional connectivity than subthreshold-depression groups in frontal, cortical and limbic areas, while a study outside the supporter list finds a monotone, dose-dependent relation of a 36-month depressive-symptom trajectory to conversion in ADNI (P-26).
method: Each second-round candidate judged yes or partly was re-read from its PDF text (ROOT/pdf/<P-id>.txt, all four present). Identity was checked: for all four, the PDF title and DOI match the summaries.md header (P-278's header is its filename, which carries the DOI) and the paper_pdf_map entry. None is in registry_duplicates.json or has a duplicate_of value, and none is in the packet's rejected_supporters list. For each, I checked whether the comparison is run within the study, whether the population and exposure are the ones the row names, whether the null comes from the paper's own statistics, whether the claim is the authors' interpretation rather than their result, and whether the sample or authors are shared with a supporter or a round-1 candidate. The standards are the ones round 1 applied: P-647 is yes for a converter-versus-stable null on a baseline score; P-1326 is partly where a continuous score tracked outcome crude but not adjusted; P-720 and P-785 are partly for the first clause only; P-578 is partly where clinical depression was excluded; presence contrasts are not severity grading (P-989). Only yes counts toward the tally.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed against the PDF (Katayama et al., Arch Gerontol Geriatr 94 (2021) 104376). Table 1 (imputed sample): 'Geriatric Depression Scale (points)* 2.6 (2.3) 3.0 (2.4) 3.3 (2.5) < 0.05a R<C' (reverters 256, maintainers 395, converters 118). Table 5 adjusted: 'GDS (points) 1.00 (0.91-1.10) > 0.05 1.01 (0.90-1.13) > 0.05' for maintainers and reverters. The table title names maintainers and reverters as the dependent categories, so the reference outcome is converters by elimination. The crude positive is reverters versus converters only; maintainers versus converters is not significant post hoc. The adjusted null is a per-point continuous GDS-15 coefficient in a model for another exposure (lifestyle class), adjusted for age (69.6 vs 76.4 years, R vs C), MMSE, walking speed and class. GDS differs by class (Table 3: 2.7, 2.3, 4.0, 3.1, p < 0.001), so the class term may absorb part of the depression signal. Against the row: the adjusted null resembles 'continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion', but the paper's own crude comparison does track outcome in the expected direction. As a supporter it would therefore not make the sentence true without qualification. This is the P-1326 pattern (crude association, adjusted null), so partly, not yes. It is closer to yes than P-1326, because P-671 prints an adjusted continuous coefficient where P-1326 has only 'data not shown'. Further limits: 'converters had GCI and/or AD at the follow-up', GCI being an MMSE score below 24, so the outcome is not dementia conversion as such; 325 of 769 lacked the second wave and were handled by multivariate normal imputation, and Table 1 and Table 5 use the imputed counts; no brain measure; all participants had MCI, so the first clause is not tested. Reporting defects that do not touch the GDS rows: Table 5 prints walking speed '6.89 (1.87-25.30) > 0.05', a CI that excludes 1 printed with a non-significant p; the methods say 'Unadjusted and adjusted models included the following covariates', although the unadjusted columns contain none. Independence: NCGG-SGS, Obu, Japan. Not a current supporter's dataset (Korea University Guro, Shanghai Brain Health Cohort, Shanghai Tongji, Florence) or a round-1 or round-2 candidate's, and no shared authors. Not a preprint.

Confirmed against the PDF (Guo, Pai, Xue and Lu, J Affect Disord 338 (2023) 449-458). Table 2: high-risk depressive symptoms (CES-D-8 >= 4) and subsequent MCI, 'Yes 1.38 (1.25, 1.53) <0.001 1.37 (1.24, 1.52) <0.001 1.20 (1.08, 1.34) 0.001' (unadjusted, minimally adjusted, fully adjusted; N = 9,317). Table 3: baseline MCI and subsequent high-risk depressive symptoms, fully adjusted '1.16 (1.01, 1.33) 0.032' (N = 9,428). This is the study's own competing-risks analysis, so the first clause (depression status is associated with MCI) is shown, in the prospective form: people free of both at baseline. Partly, for the first clause only, on the P-720 and P-785 standard. Limits: 'status' is a CES-D-8 screen, not a diagnosis; MCI is a composite-score band (7-11 of 27) from the HRS interview battery, not a clinical diagnosis; everyone with MCI or dementia at baseline was excluded, so there is no MCI prognosis, no MCI-to-dementia outcome and no brain measure, and the severity limbs are untouched. The only continuous-severity result is reported in words from a supplement not in the extract: 'participants with higher CES-D scores at baseline were more likely to have decreased trajectories of cognitive functioning' (p. 4), and 'We re-run all statistical models using continuous CES-D ... Results were consistent' (p. 8-9). That leans toward severity grading cognitive course (the P-26 side), but in a non-MCI population and on a cognitive score, not conversion, so it is context, not counter-evidence to the MCI limb. NEW DEFECT, not in the verifier note: the sample-selection text says 'At subsequent visits, those participants who scored in the dementia range have been excluded' (p. 3), while the outcome definition codes '1 = subsequent MCI [including cases with subsequent dementia ...]' (p. 3). The two are hard to reconcile, so how incident dementia-range scorers enter the outcome is unclear. This does not reverse the first-clause result. Authors' limitations: a limited composite cognitive measure; excluded participants more often had the baseline exposures; residual confounding. Independence: HRS, not the dataset of any supporter or round-1/round-2 candidate (P-785 is HCHS/SOL, P-954 is WHICAP); no shared authors. Not a preprint.

Confirmed against the PDF (Raymond-Lessard, Belanger, Hudon, Grenier and the CIMA-Q Group, J Alzheimers Dis 104(3) (2025) 720-731). Results p. 6: 'Regarding the intensity of depressive symptoms, it was not significant, U(N of SCD-P = 21; N of SCD-NP = 59) = 517.5, z = -1.20, p = 0.263.' Table 2: 'GDS +/- SD 7.43 +/- 6,66 5.46 +/- 4.91 ... 517.5, p = 0.263'; 'GDS >=3 N (%) 15 (71.4) 39 (66.1) ... 0.200, p = 0.654'. The population is SCD, not MCI, and the outcome is progression from SCD to NIA-AA MCI or probable AD, not MCI-to-dementia conversion. The row concerns MCI neurobiology and prognosis, so this is partly at most under the brief's different-population rule. The part shown: in older adults with SCD, baseline GDS-30 intensity did not separate those who developed MCI or AD within four years. It is further weakened on the P-578 range-restriction ground: 'clinical depression or an anxiety disorder' was an exclusion (p. 4), and the mean is about 6 of 30. The authors attribute the null partly to power: 'This could have increased the risk of a type II error' (p. 8). There are 21 progressors, the tests are univariate (an age-adjusted re-run is described in words only), and the progressors' mean is numerically higher (7.43 vs 5.46). The hopelessness result (p = 0.048) is one of six uncorrected subscale tests and bears on no clause. Screen-level symptoms (GDS >= 3) were no more common in progressors, but with clinical depression excluded this is not a test of the first clause. Reporting defects confirmed: z = -1.20 two-tailed gives p of about 0.23, not the printed 0.263 (the MoCA and hopelessness z/p pairs are internally consistent); Table 1 women 14 + 47 = 61, printed total '58 (72.5%)', with the text saying 58%; Table 1 prints the sex test as '0.486, p = 0.486'; Table 2 anxiety-dimension SD '.14' for SCD-P is implausible beside 1.09. None changes the GDS null. Independence: CIMA-Q (Montreal, Quebec City, Sherbrooke; part recruited from NuAge), not the dataset of any supporter or round-1/round-2 candidate; no shared authors. Not a preprint. The registry Dataset field for P-278 reads 'not reported', although the paper names CIMA-Q. That is a registry gap, not a verdict issue.

Confirmed against the PDF (Hsu et al., Alzheimers Dement (Transl Res Clin Interv) 2025;11:e70179). Table 2 (by conversion status): 'Depressive symptoms, n (%) 24 (16.2) 14 (15.7) 0.99' (remained MCI 148, progressed to dementia 89). Table 3 multivariable Cox: 'Depressive symptoms 0.86 0.46 1.60 0.64'. Population: CDR 0.5 MCI; outcome: CDR 0.5 to 1, with dementia 'further confirmed by the neurologists' (ICD-10/11). So population and outcome match the row's conversion limb. The exposure does not: it is depressive-symptom STATUS (a GDS-15 screen reported as n (%); cut-off in Table S1, not in the extract), not a continuous severity score. It therefore does not show that 'continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'. It shows the adjacent point that a two-level GDS-15 screen neither separated nor predicted MCI-to-dementia progression, crude or adjusted. Round 1 counted P-1326's categorical GDS strata as partly, so a two-category screen is partly on the same footing, not yes. NEW NOTE, not in the verifier text: the methods list 'GDS-15' among the Cox covariates, while Table 3 labels the row 'Depressive symptoms', as in the binary rows of Tables 1-2. The entry form is not stated. The CI width (0.46-1.60), set against per-point covariates such as MNA-SF (0.87-1.12), is consistent with a binary indicator. The Cox coefficient is conditional on polypharmacy (strongly protective, HR 0.49), which is itself associated with depressive symptoms (Table 1: 22.0% vs 10.9%, p 0.03), but the crude Table 2 null does not depend on that. Limits: depression is a covariate, never the exposure; prevalence is about 16%; veterans-home residents are mixed with outpatients (recruitment HR 3.38); dementia is all-cause; no brain measure; all participants have MCI, so the first clause is not tested. Denominator slips confirmed: Table 1 non-polypharmacy percentages imply 128 (58/128 = 45.3%, 68/128 = 53.1%) and polypharmacy 109 (86/109 = 78.9%, 31/109 = 28.4%) against headers of 129 and 108; Table 2 polypharmacy 78 + 31 = 109. These do not touch the Table 2 depression row (24/148 = 16.2%, 14/89 = 15.7%). Independence: Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital and Veterans Homes, Taiwan, not the dataset of any supporter or round-1/round-2 candidate; no shared authors. Not a preprint.

stated_form.method_family_check: Unchanged from round 1. The yes set spans two method families: three of the four yes supporters rest on the same low-powered univariate converter comparison (17 to 28 converters each). If H.1's requirement that method families be distinct is enforced, the stated form reaches two, not three. None of the second-round partly papers adds a method family to the yes set, because none is yes. P-671's crude part is the same kind of analysis as P-647, P-788 and P-974; its adjusted part and P-1157's are covariate coefficients in models built for other exposures.
stated_form.clause_coverage_after_round2: First clause (depression status is associated with MCI): still no yes supporter. Partly from P-720 (unadjusted, GDS-30 score of 10 or more), P-785 (anxious-depression class) and now P-646. P-646 is the strongest of the three, a prospective HRS competing-risks result (fully adjusted SHR 1.20 for a CES-D-8 screen to incident score-band MCI, and 1.16 in reverse), but its MCI is a cognitive-score band, not a clinical diagnosis. Brain limb: P-643 alone; no second-round paper has a brain measure. 'Although' clause: P-643 alone. Conversion limb: yes from P-647, P-788 and P-974 (one method family). The partly range now also holds P-671 (adjusted per-point GDS null for a GCI-or-AD outcome, but a significant crude reverter-versus-converter difference), P-1157 (binary screen null, crude and adjusted, for CDR-1 dementia) and P-278 (SCD-to-MCI/AD null, different population, depression-excluded). Counter-signals on the conversion limb: P-989 (continuous SGDS HR 1.040 per point, p 0.017), P-1326 (significant inverse crude association), P-671's crude R<C difference, and P-26 (not checked). P-646's continuous CES-D predicted steeper cognitive decline in a non-MCI population (supplement, not in the extract) and is context only.

narrowed_wording.status: not applicable: round 20 recorded no narrowed wording for VF-27, and no second-round candidate was judged against one (all n/a). The empty list and false mean that no narrowed form exists, NOT that support was counted and fell short.

tally.changed_from_round1: nothing in the yes tally. None of the four second-round candidates is refuted, and none rises to yes. P-671, P-646, P-278 and P-1157 are added to the partly list, which grows from six to ten, and to the clause-coverage notes. The stated form stays at four independent yes dataset families (P-643, P-647, P-788, P-974) and two method families. The narrowed form stays not applicable.

consequences_for_wording: The second round leaves the round-1 picture intact. Four dataset families say yes, but only through the conversion limb, and three of those four use one method. The first clause now has one more partly source (P-646, HRS) but still no yes. The conversion limb gains three weak partly nulls (P-671 adjusted, P-1157 binary, P-278 in SCD) and one more crude counter-signal (P-671's R<C difference). This reinforces the row's 'divided' framing rather than a clean 'fails to track' sentence. This record takes no position on admission. That is the operator's decision.
defects_noted: P-671 Table 5: walking speed '6.89 (1.87-25.30)' printed with '> 0.05' (a CI excluding 1 with a non-significant p); the reference outcome is not named in the table (converters by elimination); the methods say the unadjusted models 'included the following covariates' although they contain none.

P-646: the sample-selection text excludes participants scoring in the dementia range at subsequent visits, while the outcome definition codes subsequent dementia as subsequent MCI; the two statements are hard to reconcile.

P-278: GDS intensity z = -1.20 printed with p = 0.263 (two-tailed about 0.23); Table 1 women 14 + 47 = 61 against a printed total of 58 (72.5%) and '58%' in the text; the sex test is printed as '0.486, p = 0.486'; the anxiety-dimension SD '.14' is implausible; the registry Dataset field is 'not reported', although the paper names CIMA-Q.

P-1157: Table 1 percentages imply group sizes 128 and 109 against headers of 129 and 108; Table 2 polypharmacy 78 + 31 = 109; the Cox depressive-symptom row's entry form (binary or GDS-15 score) is not stated, although its CI width suggests binary.
summary: All four second-round candidates survive, but only as partly. None is refuted and none is yes. P-671 (NCGG-SGS, Obu): the adjusted per-point GDS-15 OR is null (1.00 and 1.01), but the crude reverter-versus-converter difference is significant (2.6 vs 3.3, p < 0.05), and the outcome is GCI-or-AD, not dementia; this is the P-1326 pattern. P-646 (HRS): a CES-D-8 screen predicts incident score-band MCI (adjusted SHR 1.20) and vice versa, which is partly for the first clause only; there is no MCI prognosis or brain measure. P-278 (CIMA-Q): a GDS-30 intensity null for SCD-to-MCI/AD progression (p = 0.263), in a different population, depression-excluded and 21 progressors. P-1157 (Kaohsiung veterans): the GDS-15 screen status is null for CDR-1 dementia (16.2% vs 15.7%; HR 0.86, 0.46-1.60), but it is status, not continuous severity. The tally is unchanged from round 1: the stated form has four independent yes dataset families (P-643, P-647, P-788, P-974), which reaches three on dataset-family counting, but these span only two method families. No yes supporter tests the first clause. The narrowed form is not applicable.
